why: CloudWatch metric streams continuously push metrics (including EC2 Auto Scaling group metrics) to Kinesis Data Firehose, which delivers them to S3 in near-real time. Both services are fully managed and serverless, and the mechanism sits outside the instance launch path, so launch speed is unaffected.

others.B: EMR is a managed cluster, not serverless, and adds unnecessary infrastructure to run.
others.C: A scheduled Lambda polls on a timer, so it is not near-real time and requires custom collection code.
others.D: Installing Kinesis Agent in a bootstrap script adds work to every launch and slows instance startup, violating the requirement.

tip: Metrics to S3/third parties continuously with no code: CloudWatch metric stream -> Firehose.

why: An AWS Glue ETL job is a serverless Spark environment that natively converts CSV to Parquet and scales to handle 1 GB files, and a Lambda triggered by S3 PUT events can simply start the job. This gives event-driven conversion with the least operational overhead.

others.A: Lambda has 15-minute, memory and /tmp limits that make converting hundreds of 1 GB files per hour fragile.
others.B: Running your own Spark job requires provisioning and managing a cluster, adding overhead.
others.C: Periodic Athena queries plus a crawler are not per-upload, and add extra moving parts and latency.

tip: CSV to Parquet at scale with minimal ops: Glue ETL job.

why: AWS Backup lets you create a backup plan with a daily schedule and a 2-year retention (lifecycle expiration), storing consistent RDS snapshots in a backup vault. It is centrally managed and far exceeds the 35-day maximum of RDS automated backups.

others.B: RDS automated backup retention maxes out at 35 days, and DLM manages EBS snapshots/AMIs, not RDS snapshots.
others.C: Shipping transaction logs to CloudWatch Logs does not produce consistent, restorable database backups.
others.D: DMS CDC to S3 is replication, not consistent restorable backups, and is complex to restore from.

tip: RDS retention beyond 35 days: AWS Backup plan or manual snapshots.

why: Joining FSx for Windows File Server to the self-managed on-premises Active Directory lets existing AD users and groups be used in NTFS ACLs and share permissions. Access to shares, folders and files is then enforced by the AD groups exactly as on premises.

others.A: IAM groups do not control SMB file and folder permissions; NTFS ACLs with AD identities do.
others.B: Tags do not enforce file-level access control on SMB shares.
others.C: A service-linked role governs what FSx can do in AWS, not which users can access files.

tip: FSx for Windows access control = join to AD (AWS Managed AD or self-managed).

why: CloudFront can cache multiple versions of the same object when the cache key includes a device header (such as CloudFront-Is-Mobile-Viewer or User-Agent). A Lambda@Edge function can inspect the User-Agent and return or rewrite to the device-specific object, delivering different content per device globally.

others.B: Network Load Balancers operate at layer 4 and cannot route on host headers.
others.D: Global Accelerator does not inspect HTTP headers, and NLBs cannot do host-based routing.
others.E: NLBs cannot do path-based routing; that is an ALB layer 7 feature.

tip: Device-specific content at the edge: CloudFront cache key on device headers plus Lambda@Edge/CloudFront Functions.

why: VPC peering is the cheapest way to connect two VPCs in the same Region: there is no hourly charge and same-AZ data transfer over peering is free. Add routes to the peering connection in both route tables and allow the app security group in the ElastiCache security group.

others.B: A Transit VPC requires extra infrastructure (typically VPN appliances on EC2), costing more than peering for two VPCs.
others.C: This fragment refers to the Transit VPC design, which is more expensive and complex than peering.
others.D: Another Transit VPC variant; unnecessary cost and complexity for connecting just two VPCs.

tip: Two VPCs, cost-effective connectivity: VPC peering. Many VPCs: Transit Gateway. Note options B-D are truncated in the source.

why: An ECS cluster with a service using the Fargate launch type means AWS manages the underlying compute, so there are no EC2 instances or control plane to patch or scale. Setting desired tasks to 2 or more provides availability with minimal ongoing maintenance.

others.B: Self-managing a Kubernetes control plane on EC2 is significant infrastructure to operate.
others.C: The EC2 launch type requires managing and scaling the container instances.
others.E: Self-managed Kubernetes worker nodes on EC2 are extra infrastructure to maintain.

tip: "Cannot manage infrastructure" for containers = Fargate.

why: An ALB performs health checks on its targets and only routes requests to healthy instances, while Route 53 points to the ALB with an alias record. Clients never receive an unhealthy instance IP because they only resolve the load balancer.

others.A: Simple routing records do not support health checks.
others.B: Failover routing supports only a primary and secondary, not distribution across 10 active instances.
others.C: CloudFront does not health-check EC2 origins in this way and would still need a load balancer for distributing dynamic requests.

tip: Route 53 health checks are DNS-level and cached by TTL; an ALB gives immediate per-request health awareness.

why: Placing EC2 instances in private subnets behind a public ALB keeps the servers unreachable from the internet, and using the ALB as the CloudFront origin delivers HTTPS from edge locations with lowest latency. This is both highly available and the most secure arrangement.

others.A: Instances in public subnets are needlessly exposed to the internet.
others.B: Instances in private subnets cannot be reached directly by CloudFront as an origin.
others.D: Public instances as direct origins bypass the load balancer and expose the servers.

tip: Most secure web tier: CloudFront -> public ALB -> EC2 in private subnets.

why: AWS Global Accelerator routes users over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint, using static anycast IPs. It continuously health-checks the ALB endpoints and fails over quickly, which suits latency-sensitive gaming traffic, including non-HTTP protocols.

others.B: CloudFront caching does not help a dynamic, latency-sensitive game and does not natively multi-Region fail over with health checks like this.
others.C: An S3 origin is for static content and does not route to the application ALBs.
others.D: DAX caches DynamoDB reads; it does not monitor endpoint health or redirect traffic.

tip: Multi-Region health-based routing with static IPs and low latency (TCP/UDP): Global Accelerator.

why: Kinesis Data Firehose is fully managed, can encrypt data and convert records to Apache Parquet before delivering to S3, and Kinesis Data Analytics (now Managed Service for Apache Flink) analyzes the stream in near-real time. Both are serverless, giving the least operational overhead.

others.A: Kinesis Data Streams cannot write directly to S3 and adding Lambda glue increases overhead.
others.B: Data Streams cannot store to S3 directly, and EMR is a cluster to manage.
others.C: EMR adds cluster management overhead compared with serverless Kinesis Data Analytics.

tip: Firehose: managed delivery to S3 with built-in Parquet/ORC format conversion.

why: Placing Amazon ElastiCache in front of RDS caches frequently read score data in memory, offloading reads and cutting latency. It improves user experience with minimal change to the existing architecture.

others.B: This option text is an artifact of the source data, not a real solution.
others.C: Moving to Lambda changes the compute tier and does nothing for database read performance.
others.D: Migrating to DynamoDB is a major architectural change, contrary to the minimal-change requirement.

tip: Read-heavy RDS bottleneck: ElastiCache or read replicas.

why: An RDS read replica serves the analysts' read-only SQL queries from a separate instance, removing load from the primary. The analysts keep using SQL against the same schema, and the web application needs no changes.

others.A: DynamoDB is NoSQL, so analysts' SQL queries would need rewriting, plus an export pipeline.
others.B: ElastiCache is a cache, not a store analysts can run ad hoc SQL queries against.
others.D: Redshift requires building a data loading pipeline and is more change than needed.

tip: Offload read-only reporting from RDS: read replica.

why: Client-side encryption encrypts the data before it leaves the client, so it is already encrypted at rest when uploaded, and the upload uses HTTPS for encryption in transit. Only client-side encryption meets the 'encrypted before upload' requirement.

others.B: Server-side encryption encrypts after S3 receives the data, not before upload.
others.C: SSE-S3 enforcement still encrypts only after arrival in S3.
others.D: Default KMS bucket encryption is server-side and happens after upload.

tip: "Encrypt before uploading" = client-side encryption.

why: Scheduled scaling raises the Auto Scaling group's capacity at a set time (just before 1 AM) because the peak is predictable, so capacity is ready when jobs start. A scheduled action can then lower capacity, letting the group scale down afterwards, which is cost-effective.

others.A: Raising minimum capacity keeps instances running all day, wasting money.
others.B: Maximum capacity only caps scaling; it does not speed up reaching desired capacity.
others.D: Larger step adjustments still react after load appears and do not pre-provision for a known schedule.

tip: Predictable recurring load: scheduled scaling (or predictive scaling).

why: The intended answer (split across options B and C because of truncated text) is to front the ALB with an Amazon API Gateway API using the HTTP integration type and enable API caching keyed on the Accept-Language header. Cached language-specific responses are served quickly without rebuilding the architecture in other Regions.

others.A: Moving to S3 replaces the dynamic website, which the company does not want to re-architect.
others.C: This truncated text is the first half of the keyed solution (API Gateway integrated with the ALB) and is incomplete on its own.
others.D: Running NGINX cache servers in every Region is effectively recreating infrastructure across Regions with high operational effort.

tip: Options in this question are garbled in the source; CloudFront caching on Accept-Language would be the more common real-world choice.

why: Aurora global database replicates to the secondary Region with typically under 1 second of lag using storage-level replication, keeping the DR database current. A warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the infrastructure that can scale up immediately, giving a lower RTO than pilot light.

others.A: Pilot light keeps only core components running, so application servers must be started and scaled, giving a higher RTO than warm standby.
others.C: RDS Multi-AZ is within a single Region and does not replicate to a DR Region.
others.D: Multi-AZ provides no cross-Region copy of the database, so it cannot serve a DR Region.

tip: DR RTO order (fastest to slowest): multi-site active/active, warm standby, pilot light, backup and restore.

why: Copying AMIs to a secondary Region and using CloudFormation to deploy the infrastructure on demand uses almost no resources during normal operation, and a templated stack can be launched well within a 4-hour RTO. CloudFormation is the managed, repeatable way to do this, making it the most operationally efficient.

others.A: Custom Lambda scripts for infrastructure deployment are more effort to build and maintain than CloudFormation.
others.C: Keeping instances running in a second Region all the time consumes the most resources.
others.D: Always-on instances in another AZ use extra resources and do not protect against a Regional outage.

tip: Backup and restore plus IaC (CloudFormation) satisfies RTOs of hours at minimal cost.

why: The keyed answer lowers the target tracking CPU threshold and reduces cooldown so the group starts adding instances earlier and faster as morning load ramps, while still scaling only as much as demand requires. This addresses the slow start while keeping cost to a minimum versus jumping straight to 20 instances.

others.A: Forcing desired capacity to 20 provisions full capacity regardless of actual demand, which may cost more than necessary.
others.B: Step scaling works but requires managing step adjustments and alarms; target tracking is simpler and self-adjusting.
others.D: Setting minimum and maximum to 20 locks the group at 20 instances and prevents scaling down during the day.

tip: Many experts prefer a scheduled action (A) for predictable daily ramps; know both arguments.

why: RDS storage autoscaling automatically grows the Oracle instance's storage when free space runs low, with no migration needed. Adding a target tracking policy on average CPU to the Auto Scaling group lets EC2 capacity scale automatically with unpredictable traffic growth.

others.B: Aurora does not support Oracle PL/SQL, so migration would require code changes.
others.C: An alarm only notifies; it does not automatically add storage.
others.E: Free memory is not a default EC2 metric (needs the CloudWatch agent) and is a less suitable scaling signal than CPU here.

tip: RDS storage running out: enable storage autoscaling with a maximum storage threshold.

why: Amazon S3 is far cheaper per GB than EFS Standard for storing a large, growing video library. Instances can copy files temporarily to an EBS volume for processing, so only working data occupies block storage while S3 holds everything durably.

others.A: Storage Gateway is for hybrid on-premises access and adds cost and complexity for a cloud-native workload.
others.B: Volume Gateway serves iSCSI volumes to on-premises hosts and is not a cost fix for EC2 in AWS.
others.C: Keeping content on EFS and then also copying to EBS keeps the expensive EFS storage and adds more.

tip: Cost reduction for bulk storage usually means S3 (with lifecycle tiers); EFS IA/archive classes are another option.

why: DynamoDB delivers single-digit millisecond latency at high traffic and can model hierarchical data with composite keys, and exporting to S3 lets Macie scan it. Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data like financial information in S3, and its findings sent through EventBridge to an SNS topic provide email notifications.

others.A: Redshift is an analytics warehouse, not designed for minimum-latency high-traffic lookups.
others.C: Sending events to Lambda does not by itself deliver email notifications; SNS is the direct way.
others.D: Athena and QuickSight provide analysis dashboards but do not detect sensitive data or send email alerts.

tip: Sensitive data/PII discovery in S3 = Macie; email alert = EventBridge -> SNS.

why: AWS Backup supports DynamoDB with a scheduled monthly backup rule, a lifecycle transition to cold storage after 6 months, and a 7-year retention period, all managed centrally. This meets every compliance requirement without custom code.

others.B: DynamoDB on-demand backups are not stored as S3 objects you manage, so S3 Lifecycle and Glacier transitions cannot be applied.
others.C: Custom scripts add operational burden, and native DynamoDB backups have no cold storage tier outside AWS Backup.
others.D: The CLI create-backup command cannot set cold storage transitions or expiration.

tip: Retention plus cold-storage lifecycle for backups = AWS Backup plan.

why: Amazon Athena runs standard SQL directly against CloudFront logs stored in S3 without loading data, and Amazon QuickSight connects to Athena to build visualizations and dashboards. This is the serverless, purpose-built combination for log analytics and visualization.

others.A: AWS Glue is for ETL and cataloging, not visualization.
others.C: DynamoDB does not query files in S3 with standard SQL, and Glue does not visualize.
others.D: DynamoDB cannot analyze S3 log files with SQL.

tip: Query logs in S3 = Athena; visualize = QuickSight.

why: RDS Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ, so committed transactions exist on both and the RPO is effectively zero. On failover no committed data is lost, meeting an RPO of under 1 second.

others.B: RDS has no instance auto scaling within an AZ, and it would not affect RPO.
others.C: Read replicas use asynchronous replication, so lag can exceed 1 second and data can be lost.
others.D: DMS CDC is asynchronous and not designed as a sub-second RPO HA mechanism.

tip: Synchronous replication (Multi-AZ) = near-zero RPO; async replicas = possible data loss.

why: The intended answer (option text missing in the source) is to configure the EC2 instances' security group to allow inbound traffic only from the ALB's security group. Referencing the ALB security group permits only the load balancer to reach the instances and blocks all other sources inside or outside the subnet.

others.A: Routing internet traffic to private IPs bypasses the ALB and increases exposure.
others.C: Moving instances to public subnets with Elastic IPs exposes them directly to the internet.
others.D: Opening the ALB security group to any TCP port weakens security and does not restrict access to the instances.

tip: Security group referencing another security group is the standard way to allow only the ALB to reach targets.

why: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP provides a single file system that is accessible simultaneously over NFS and SMB (multiprotocol). The Linux simulation and Windows visualization apps on EC2 can share the same data without duplication or code changes.

others.A: Rewriting for Lambda and using S3 requires code changes and Lambda does not run Windows desktop apps.
others.B: FSx File Gateway provides on-premises SMB access to FSx for Windows, not NFS, and ECS migration needs changes.
others.C: SQS is a message queue, not a shared file system, so applications would need code changes.

tip: Need both NFS and SMB on one file system = FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

why: Cost Explorer can group and filter costs by dimensions and cost allocation tags (for example a user or department tag) and the resulting report can be downloaded as CSV. It is the most efficient built-in way to produce a cost-by-user report for budget planning.

others.A: Athena requires setting up CUR delivery and writing queries, which is more work.
others.C: The billing dashboard bill is not broken down by user.
others.D: AWS Budgets sends alerts on thresholds; it does not produce an itemized report by user.

tip: Ad-hoc cost reports by tag/service = Cost Explorer; detailed line items = CUR + Athena.

why: API Gateway plus Lambda is serverless and billed per request, so fewer than 100 visits a month cost almost nothing (often within the free tier). The Lambda function calls Amazon SES to email the submitted form, and the static S3 site stays unchanged.

others.A: Running ECS continuously costs far more than needed for a handful of submissions.
others.C: Lightsail adds an always-on server and WorkMail is a mailbox service, not a form email sender.
others.D: An always-on EC2 LAMP instance costs more and adds server management.

tip: Low-traffic dynamic feature on a static S3 site: API Gateway + Lambda.

why: CloudFront is serving cached copies of the old objects until their TTL expires. Creating a CloudFront invalidation (for example for /* or changed paths) forces edge locations to fetch the updated files from S3 so the new deployment appears.

others.A: An ALB does not serve S3 static content and does not affect CloudFront caching.
others.B: Caching the database layer does nothing about stale static files at the CDN edge.
others.D: Certificate validation is unrelated to stale content.

tip: Deployed but not visible behind CloudFront = invalidate cache or use versioned file names.

why: SQL Server native backups and Data Quality Services require full control of SQL Server, so the database runs on EC2 rather than RDS. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed SMB share for the Windows tiers to exchange files.

others.A: FSx File Gateway is for giving on-premises clients cached access to FSx, not for sharing between EC2 tiers.
others.C: RDS for SQL Server does not support Data Quality Services, and EFS is NFS-based for Linux, not Windows.
others.D: RDS lacks DQS, and an io2 EBS volume is not a general shared file system for Windows tiers.

tip: Need SQL Server features RDS lacks = SQL Server on EC2; Windows file sharing = FSx for Windows.

why: Amazon EFS is a managed NFS file system that multiple Linux instances can mount concurrently using standard file system semantics. The application continues to use file paths, so no changes are needed.

others.A: S3 is object storage accessed via API, which would require application changes.
others.B: CloudFront with S3 is for content delivery, not a mounted shared file store.
others.D: Standard gp3 EBS volumes cannot be attached to multiple instances (Multi-Attach is io1/io2 only and needs a cluster-aware file system).

tip: Shared file system for Linux EC2 = EFS; for Windows = FSx for Windows.

why: Assigning an IAM execution role to the Lambda function provides temporary, automatically rotated credentials. Scoping the attached policy to read access on only that specific bucket follows least privilege, making it the most secure approach.

others.A: A bucket policy alone works but is not the standard least-privilege identity approach, and still needs a principal; the execution role is preferred.
others.C: Embedding long-term access keys in code is insecure.
others.D: Granting read on all buckets violates least privilege.

tip: AWS service needs access = IAM role with least-privilege policy, never embedded keys.

why: A mix of On-Demand for the baseline and Spot Instances for scalable capacity reduces cost significantly (Spot can be up to 90% cheaper) with no long-term commitment. Auto Scaling groups support mixed instances policies to combine both.

others.A: Dedicated Instances cost more and do nothing for savings.
others.B: On-Demand only has no commitment but misses Spot savings.
others.D: Reserved Instances require a 1- or 3-year commitment.

tip: "No long-term commitment" rules out RIs and Savings Plans.

why: CloudFront signed cookies control access to multiple files without changing URLs, which suits users with hardcoded URLs. Signed URLs embed the authorization in the URL itself, which suits the custom HTTP client that cannot handle cookies. Together they cover both user groups with the least impact.

others.C: AWS AppSync is a managed GraphQL API service, not a CloudFront content access control.
others.D: JWTs would need custom validation logic at the edge and client changes.
others.E: Secrets Manager stores secrets; it does not control viewer access to CloudFront content.

tip: No cookie support -> signed URLs; cannot change URLs -> signed cookies.

why: Kinesis Data Streams with Kinesis Data Analytics transforming the stream and Firehose delivering to S3, queried by Athena, is a complete streaming pipeline. Likewise MSK for ingestion with AWS Glue streaming ETL transforming and writing to S3, then Athena for SQL, also meets all requirements.

others.C: DMS is for database migration/replication, not ingesting real-time streams from many sources.
others.D: The RDS query editor cannot query data stored in S3.
others.E: The RDS query editor cannot query S3 data, so SQL over the transformed data fails.

tip: SQL over data in S3 = Athena (or Redshift Spectrum).

why: A Storage Gateway stored volume gateway keeps the complete dataset on premises for low-latency local access while asynchronously backing it up to AWS as EBS snapshots. Transfers are automatic and encrypted in transit, meeting all the requirements.

others.A: Snowball is a one-time offline migration device and does not provide ongoing backup or local access.
others.B: Snowball Edge is for transfer or edge compute, not a continuous backup solution with full local access.
others.C: Cached volumes keep only frequently accessed data locally, so not all data remains locally accessible.

tip: All data local + async backup = stored volumes; only hot data local = cached volumes.

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 adds a route in the VPC route table so traffic to S3 stays on the AWS network and never traverses the internet. Gateway endpoints for S3 have no additional charge.

others.A: A private hosted zone handles DNS names and does not change the network path to S3.
others.C: A NAT gateway sends traffic to S3's public endpoints via the internet gateway path and adds cost.
others.D: Site-to-Site VPN connects networks, not a VPC to an S3 bucket.

tip: Private S3/DynamoDB access from a VPC = gateway endpoint (free).

why: S3 Object Lambda lets you attach a Lambda function to S3 GET requests via an access point so data is transformed (for example PII redacted) on the fly before it reaches the application. One copy of the data serves all three apps, giving the least operational overhead.

others.A: Building and operating a custom proxy layer adds significant overhead.
others.C: Maintaining three transformed copies requires ongoing processing pipelines and extra storage.
others.D: Three DynamoDB tables duplicate data and require custom transformation pipelines.

tip: Modify or redact S3 data per requester without copies = S3 Object Lambda.

why: Peered VPCs must have non-overlapping CIDR blocks, and a VPC's CIDR must be between /16 and /28. 10.0.1.0/24 does not overlap 192.168.0.0/24 and is valid; it is the smallest valid option offered.

others.A: A /32 is not a valid VPC CIDR size (minimum is /28).
others.B: This overlaps the development VPC exactly, so peering is not allowed.
others.C: A /32 is not a valid VPC CIDR size.

tip: VPC CIDR range: /16 to /28; peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs.

why: An Auto Scaling group attached to the existing target group with a target tracking policy on ASGAverageCPUUtilization at 50% automatically adds instances during surges and removes them when CPU is low. Minimum 2 and maximum 6 keep availability while optimizing cost.

others.A: A Lambda that only terminates instances cannot add capacity during surges.
others.C: Without a scaling policy, the group never scales with demand.
others.D: Manual scaling after email alerts is not automated.

tip: Keep a metric near a value automatically = target tracking.

why: Subnets are confined to a single Availability Zone, so you create one subnet per AZ and spread the Auto Scaling group across both. Enabling RDS Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby in the second AZ with automatic failover, making both tiers highly available.

others.A: Connecting the DB instance to each network does not create a standby; it remains a single point of failure.
others.B: Subnets cannot span Availability Zones.
others.D: A subnet cannot extend across Availability Zones.

tip: Subnet = one AZ. DB HA = Multi-AZ.

why: FSx for Lustre on persistent SSD storage delivers sub-millisecond latency and hundreds of GBps throughput for hundreds of Linux clients. Linking it to an S3 bucket lets it import raw data from and export results back to S3.

others.A: Tiering policy ALL moves data to the capacity pool tier, which cannot provide sub-millisecond latency, and ONTAP is not built for 6 GBps HPC parallel throughput.
others.C: HDD storage cannot provide sub-millisecond latency.
others.D: FSx for ONTAP is not designed for this HPC parallel throughput profile (option text truncated).
others.E: This is a fragment of option D and is not a complete solution.

tip: HPC, Linux, high throughput, S3 integration = FSx for Lustre (SSD for low latency).

why: A 24/7 application gets the largest savings from Reserved Instances for the EC2 tier. Aurora storage automatically grows up to 128 TiB as the database expands, and Aurora Reserved Instances discount the always-on database compute.

others.A: Spot Instances can be interrupted, unsuitable for a 24/7 legacy app, and S3 is not a database replacement.
others.B: On-Demand RDS costs more than reserved capacity for a 24/7 database.
others.D: On-Demand EC2 costs more than Reserved Instances for constant usage.

tip: Steady 24/7 usage = Reserved Instances or Savings Plans.

why: AWS DataSync transfers data to FSx for Windows File Server with parallel, accelerated transfers and lets you set a bandwidth limit on tasks. 30 TB in 5 days needs about 0.56 Gbps, which fits on the shared 1 Gbps link with throttling.

others.A: Snowcone holds only 8-14 TB and shipping adds time, so it cannot carry 30 TB in time.
others.B: FSx File Gateway provides cached on-premises access to FSx, not a bulk migration service.
others.D: Transfer Family provides SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints for S3/EFS, not FSx for Windows migration.

tip: Online migration with bandwidth throttling into S3/EFS/FSx = DataSync.

why: CloudFront caches and delivers the video from edge locations close to mobile users, reducing buffering and scaling automatically. The question asks for two choices; the second intended choice is Amazon Elastic Transcoder (C), which converts raw videos to mobile-friendly formats with no servers to manage.

others.B: Replicating files across Regions with DataSync does not fix large raw formats or edge delivery.
others.C: Transcoding to mobile formats is also needed, but this keyed answer lists only A (Elastic Transcoder is now superseded by AWS Elemental MediaConvert).
others.D: Running EC2 caching fleets in Local Zones adds heavy operational overhead versus CloudFront.
others.E: Self-managed EC2 transcoding adds operational overhead versus a managed transcoding service.

tip: Video for mobile: transcode (MediaConvert) + deliver via CloudFront.
flag: The question asks for two answers but the key lists only A; the accepted answer is A and C (CloudFront plus managed transcoding).

why: ECS service auto scaling uses AWS Application Auto Scaling; a target tracking policy on CPU or memory utilization automatically adds Fargate tasks under load and removes them when utilization falls, reducing cost. It is fully managed with no custom code.

others.A: EC2 Auto Scaling manages EC2 instances, and Fargate tasks have no instances to scale.
others.B: A custom Lambda scaler adds code and maintenance versus built-in service auto scaling.
others.C: EC2 Auto Scaling does not scale Fargate tasks.

tip: Scale ECS services, DynamoDB, Aurora replicas, etc. = Application Auto Scaling.

why: AWS DataSync is a managed service that copies data between NFS file systems (including EFS) across Regions, with scheduling, encryption, integrity checks and incremental transfers. Periodic transfers need no infrastructure to manage.

others.B: Snowball devices are for offline transfer and impractical for periodic Region-to-Region copies.
others.C: An SFTP server on EC2 must be built, secured and maintained.
others.D: DMS migrates databases, not file systems.

tip: Scheduled file copies between storage systems/Regions = DataSync.

why: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed native Windows file system that SMB clients can access directly. It handles patching, backups and availability, unlike a self-managed file server.

others.A: DataSync moves data; it does not present a mountable shared file system.
others.B: A Windows file share on EC2 is self-managed, not fully managed.
others.D: S3 is object storage and is not natively accessible over SMB.

tip: Managed SMB = FSx for Windows (or FSx for ONTAP).

why: A cluster placement group packs instances close together in one Availability Zone for the lowest latency and highest network throughput. Keeping everything in the same AZ also avoids inter-AZ data transfer charges, making it cost-effective.

others.B: Spreading across AZs incurs inter-AZ data transfer charges and higher latency, and partition groups target fault isolation.
others.C: Multi-AZ Auto Scaling increases cross-AZ traffic costs and latency.
others.D: Step scaling across AZs does not reduce latency or data transfer charges.

tip: Lowest latency/highest throughput between instances = cluster placement group (single AZ).

why: Volume Gateway in cached mode presents iSCSI volumes whose primary data lives in S3, while only frequently or recently accessed data is cached locally. This minimizes on-premises iSCSI storage scaling.

others.A: S3 File Gateway presents NFS/SMB file shares, not iSCSI block storage.
others.B: Tape Gateway provides virtual tape libraries for backup software, not general iSCSI volumes.
others.C: Stored volumes keep the full dataset on premises, so local storage still needs to scale.

tip: iSCSI + only hot data local = cached volumes.

why: In a consolidated billing (Organizations) setup, the management/payer account can view Trusted Advisor recommendations across linked accounts in one place. The Amazon RDS Idle DB Instances check identifies instances with no connections that can be stopped or deleted to cut RDS costs.

others.A: Checking each account separately is less efficient than viewing all from the consolidated billing account.
others.C: The keyed answer prefers the idle instance check; RI optimization is a commitment-based recommendation rather than a direct waste check for these instances.
others.E: Redshift reserved node optimization is unrelated to RDS.

tip: Trusted Advisor cost checks include idle RDS instances, underutilized EC2 and RI optimization.

why: S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics include activity metrics (such as GET request counts and bytes downloaded) per bucket in a ready-made dashboard, making cold or unused buckets easy to identify. It requires only enabling the feature, so operational overhead is lowest.

others.B: The basic S3 console dashboard does not show per-bucket access pattern analysis.
others.C: BucketSizeBytes measures storage size, not access, and Athena analysis adds work.
others.D: CloudTrail data events plus log analysis is costly and requires building queries.

tip: Org-wide S3 usage and activity insights = S3 Storage Lens.

why: CloudFront caches the datasets at edge locations near customers in North America and Europe, improving performance, and data transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free while CloudFront egress is generally cheaper than S3 internet egress. CloudFront signed URLs keep purchase-based access control.

others.A: Transfer Acceleration adds per-GB charges, increasing rather than reducing transfer cost.
others.C: A replicated bucket doubles storage and adds replication transfer costs.
others.D: Streaming through EC2 adds compute and data transfer cost and effort.

tip: Reduce S3 egress cost and latency for global downloads = CloudFront with OAC and signed URLs.

why: A single SNS topic with SQS queue subscriptions and message filter policies fans out each quote to the queue for its type. SQS durably stores messages (retention up to 14 days), so nothing is lost and backends can process within 24 hours, all with fully managed services.

others.A: Kinesis requires shard management and KCL consumers, which is more maintenance for simple queuing.
others.B: SNS to Lambda has no durable queue for buffering; failed deliveries can be lost without extra DLQ setup.
others.D: Using OpenSearch as a message queue is inappropriate and costly to maintain.

tip: Route messages by attribute to different consumers durably = SNS filter policies + SQS fan-out.

why: Adding EC2 instances as resources in an AWS Backup plan creates AMIs that capture both the instance configuration and all attached EBS volumes. The plan runs nightly and can copy backups to another Region for cross-Region recovery, all without custom code.

others.A: Custom Lambda scripts add maintenance and EBS snapshots alone do not capture instance configuration.
others.C: Backing up only EBS volumes misses the EC2 instance configuration.
others.D: Copying to another AZ does not provide cross-Region recovery, and custom code adds overhead.

tip: Back up the EC2 instance resource (not just volumes) to capture configuration.

why: CloudFront scales to millions of users and streams content from edge locations, and signed URLs restrict content to authorized users with expiry times. This is the standard pattern for private content delivery to mobile apps.

others.A: A public S3 bucket exposes content to everyone, and KMS does not stream content.
others.B: IPsec VPN from millions of mobile devices is impractical.
others.D: Client VPN for millions of consumer users is impractical and costly.

tip: Authorized access to media at scale = CloudFront signed URLs/cookies.

why: Aurora Serverless for MySQL automatically scales capacity (ACUs) with demand, so no instance type must be chosen, and it suits infrequent, variable access. It is MySQL-compatible, so migration (for example with DMS) can occur with minimal downtime.

others.A: Provisioned Aurora requires choosing an instance class.
others.C: Redshift Spectrum queries S3 data for analytics; it is not an OLTP MySQL database.
others.D: RDS for MySQL requires selecting an instance type.

tip: "No instance type selection" / unpredictable usage = Aurora Serverless.

why: Amazon Inspector continuously scans EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure, producing detailed findings. A Lambda function can automate report generation and distribution (Inspector v2 now uses the SSM agent rather than a separate Inspector agent).

others.A: AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks; it does not scan for vulnerabilities.
others.B: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3, not vulnerabilities on EC2.
others.C: GuardDuty detects threats from logs and activity; it does not perform vulnerability scans.

tip: Vulnerability/CVE scanning = Inspector; threat detection = GuardDuty; PII in S3 = Macie.

why: Lambda natively polls SQS through an event source mapping and scales concurrency automatically as the queue grows. You pay only for invocations instead of an always-running instance, reducing operational cost.

others.A: A larger instance costs more and still has fixed capacity.
others.B: Turning off the instance does not handle growing message volume.
others.D: Run Command still requires EC2 and does not scale automatically with queue depth.

tip: SQS processing without servers = Lambda event source mapping.

why: A scheduled AWS Glue ETL job is serverless and can read the CSV files from S3, transform them, and load them into Amazon Redshift, which the COTS application can query. It requires no infrastructure management.

others.B: Custom Python scripts on EC2 require managing servers, and .sql files are not a queryable format for the COTS app.
others.C: DynamoDB is not a data source the COTS application supports.
others.D: Launching EMR clusters adds operational overhead compared with serverless Glue.

tip: Serverless ETL from S3 into Redshift = AWS Glue.

why: CloudTrail records who made which API calls, such as launching instances or changing security group rules, providing an audit trail. AWS Config records configuration history and evaluates rules (for example desired instance types or restricted security group rules) to flag noncompliant changes.

others.B: Data lifecycle policies manage EBS snapshots/AMIs, not configuration auditing.
others.C: Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks, not change tracking and auditing.
others.E: Restoring configurations with CloudFormation does not track or audit changes.

tip: Who did it = CloudTrail; what changed and is it compliant = Config.

why: Systems Manager Session Manager provides browser or CLI shell access to instances through the SSM Agent using IAM for authorization, with no SSH keys, open inbound ports or bastions. Sessions can be logged, and it scales to hundreds of instances with little administration.

others.B: STS issues temporary AWS credentials, not SSH keys.
others.C: Bastions still rely on shared SSH keys and add servers to manage.
others.D: Building a Cognito plus Lambda key system is complex custom work.

tip: Remove SSH keys/bastions = Session Manager (or EC2 Instance Connect).

why: Kinesis Data Streams durably stores records across AZs as soon as they are put, so a reboot of the producer EC2 instance does not lose already-sent data, and it scales with shards well beyond 1 MB/s. Kinesis Data Analytics queries the stream in near-real time.

others.B: Firehose buffers before loading into Redshift, adding latency, and Redshift is less suited to near-real-time queries.
others.C: Instance store data is lost on stop or failure, and Firehose buffering delays queries.
others.D: Redis pub/sub does not persist messages, so data can still be lost.

tip: Durable real-time ingestion with SQL analytics on the stream = Kinesis Data Streams + Data Analytics/Flink.

why: A bucket policy that denies s3:PutObject when the x-amz-server-side-encryption header is missing ensures every upload requests server-side encryption. (Since January 2023, S3 also encrypts all new objects with SSE-S3 by default.)

others.A: The x-amz-acl header controls access permissions, not encryption.
others.B: Requiring a private ACL does not ensure encryption.
others.C: aws:SecureTransport enforces encryption in transit, not at rest.

tip: Enforce encryption at rest in a policy = deny PutObject without x-amz-server-side-encryption.

why: Placing a message on an SQS queue decouples upload from thumbnail generation, so the application can immediately confirm receipt to the user while workers process thumbnails asynchronously. SQS buffers requests between tiers reliably.

others.A: A single Lambda generating the thumbnail and alerting ties the response to the 60-second processing.
others.B: Step Functions orchestrates workflows but the user notification happens only after completion, not on receipt.
others.D: This notifies the user after thumbnail generation, not quickly when the image is received.

tip: Respond fast, process later = decouple with SQS.

why: API Gateway provides a highly available, managed HTTPS endpoint that invokes Lambda to process each badge message and store results in DynamoDB. All components are serverless and Multi-AZ, and the security team can analyze the stored data.

others.A: A single EC2 instance is a single point of failure.
others.C: Route 53 is DNS and cannot invoke Lambda or receive HTTPS messages.
others.D: Sensors send HTTPS messages; writing directly to S3 over VPN needs device changes and provides no processing.

tip: HTTPS ingestion serverless pattern = API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB.

why: A Volume Gateway stored volume keeps the full dataset on premises for immediate, low-latency access while asynchronously backing up to S3 as EBS snapshots. It presents iSCSI like the existing device, so change is minimal, and snapshots can be restored to EBS on EC2 for DR.

others.A: S3 File Gateway is NFS/SMB, not iSCSI, and a 10 TB cache would not keep all data local.
others.B: Cached volumes keep only hot data locally, so some file access would incur latency (option text partly merged).
others.C: A 10 TB cache for hundreds of TB means most data is not locally available.

tip: Immediate local access to all data with AWS backup = stored volumes. Several options here are truncated in the source.

why: Cognito identity pools exchange the user pool JWT for temporary AWS credentials by assuming an IAM role. Configuring the identity pool's authenticated role with permissions for the protected S3 bucket lets users access the content.

others.B: ACLs are legacy and do not grant access based on Cognito-authenticated identities.
others.C: S3 now provides strong read-after-write consistency, so consistency is not the cause.
others.D: Attribute mappings alone do not grant AWS permissions without a proper IAM role.

tip: User pool = authentication (JWT); identity pool = AWS credentials via IAM role.

why: After 30 days, S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves each object between access tiers based on its own inconsistent pattern with no retrieval fees, keeping multi-AZ resilience. A lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads removes orphaned parts that otherwise incur storage charges.

others.C: Expired object delete markers only exist with versioning, which is not described here.
others.D: Standard-IA charges retrieval fees, which can be costly with unpredictable access.
others.E: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, reducing resilience.

tip: Unknown or changing access patterns = Intelligent-Tiering.

why: AWS Network Firewall inspects outbound traffic routed through it and supports stateful domain list rule groups that allow only specified domain names (via SNI/Host headers) and deny everything else. Routing the private subnet's egress through the firewall enforces the approved-repository policy.

others.B: ALB listener rules handle inbound requests to targets, not outbound internet filtering.
others.C: Security groups filter by IP, port and protocol only; they cannot specify URLs or domains.
others.D: An ALB does not proxy outbound traffic from instances to the internet.

tip: Outbound filtering by domain/URL = Network Firewall (or a proxy); security groups cannot do FQDNs.

why: CloudFront offloads static content from the API, and an SQS queue buffers the sudden surge of sales requests so the backend workers process them asynchronously at their own pace. Messages are stored durably, ensuring every request is eventually processed.

others.A: Caching dynamic content does not help sales requests, and a fixed instance increase may still be overwhelmed.
others.B: Auto Scaling takes minutes to react to a sudden spike, so requests can fail meanwhile without buffering.
others.C: ElastiCache cannot sit in front of an ALB, and caching sales transactions is inappropriate.

tip: "Ensure all requests are processed" during spikes = buffer with SQS.

why: Amazon Inspector automatically and continuously scans EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities across the fleet. Systems Manager Patch Manager applies patches on a schedule via maintenance windows and reports each instance's patch compliance status.

others.A: Macie scans S3 for sensitive data, not EC2 vulnerabilities, and per-instance cron jobs give no central reporting.
others.B: GuardDuty detects threats, not software vulnerabilities, and Session Manager is for shell access, not scheduled patching.
others.C: Detective investigates security findings; it does not scan for vulnerabilities, and EventBridge alone does not patch.

tip: Scan = Inspector; patch + compliance report = Patch Manager.

why: RDS encryption at rest is enabled at instance creation using an AWS KMS key (AWS managed or customer managed), encrypting storage, backups, snapshots and replicas. Creating a KMS key and enabling encryption meets the requirement.

others.B: RDS does not use keys stored in Secrets Manager for storage encryption.
others.C: ACM certificates and SSL/TLS protect data in transit, not at rest.
others.D: IAM server certificates and TLS address encryption in transit, not at rest.

tip: At rest = KMS; in transit = TLS. Encrypt an existing unencrypted RDS DB via encrypted snapshot copy and restore.

why: At 70% of 15 Mbps (about 10.5 Mbps), transferring 20 TB would take roughly 176 days, far beyond 30 days. AWS Snowball moves the data offline on a physical device, meeting the deadline without using the network.

others.B: DataSync still uses the limited network link and cannot move 20 TB in 30 days.
others.C: A VPN uses the same constrained bandwidth.
others.D: Transfer Acceleration optimizes the path but cannot exceed the local bandwidth limit.

tip: Calculate transfer time: if it exceeds the deadline, use Snow Family.

why: FSx for Windows File Server provides scalable managed SMB storage, and joining it to the on-premises Active Directory keeps existing authorization via NTFS permissions. AWS Client VPN gives remote employees encrypted access to download files securely.

others.A: A file server in a public subnet exposes sensitive data to the internet and still needs capacity management.
others.C: Signed URLs can be shared with anyone and do not tie access to authorized directory users.
others.D: There is no public VPC endpoint, and this does not address secure SMB file access.

tip: Remote secure access to private file shares = FSx + AD + Client VPN.

why: The batch runs at a known time (midnight on the first day of each month), so a scheduled scaling action adds capacity just before it starts, preventing the instant CPU spike from disrupting the application. Capacity can be reduced afterwards with another scheduled action.

others.A: CloudFront caching does not help a CPU-bound backend batch calculation.
others.B: Simple scaling reacts after CPU spikes and has cooldowns, so the application is disrupted first.
others.D: ElastiCache does not offload a compute-heavy batch calculation.

tip: Known recurring spike = scheduled scaling.

why: AWS Transfer Family provides a fully managed SFTP endpoint backed by Amazon S3 and supports Active Directory authentication through AWS Directory Service (AD Connector or Managed AD). The customer keeps using its SFTP client unchanged.

others.B: DMS migrates databases, not files over SFTP.
others.C: DataSync is not an SFTP server for clients and does not use AD for customer downloads.
others.D: A self-managed SFTP server on EC2 adds operational overhead.

tip: Managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP into S3 or EFS = Transfer Family.

why: EBS fast snapshot restore makes volumes created from the snapshot fully initialized at creation, avoiding the first-access latency of lazy loading from S3. Building the AMI from that snapshot gives Auto Scaling instances full disk performance immediately.

others.A: Registering an AMI and swapping it with Step Functions does not remove volume initialization latency.
others.C: DLM automates AMI creation and retention but does not reduce initialization latency.
others.D: AWS Backup and EventBridge do not provide pre-warmed volumes.

tip: Avoid EBS restore latency/pre-warming = fast snapshot restore.

why: Secrets Manager stores credentials encrypted with a KMS key and has native rotation for Aurora/RDS credentials using AWS-provided rotation functions. Setting a 14-day rotation schedule meets the requirement with the least effort.

others.B: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation, so a custom Lambda must be written and maintained.
others.C: Storing credentials in files on EFS plus custom rotation is error-prone and high effort.
others.D: Credentials files in S3 plus custom rotation and regular downloads add operational effort.

tip: Encrypted + automatic rotation of DB credentials = Secrets Manager.

why: Aurora Replicas share the cluster's storage volume, so replica lag is typically well under 100 ms, and Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes replicas automatically. Aurora MySQL is compatible with the application, keeping code changes minimal while lowering operational overhead.

others.B: DynamoDB RCUs require rewriting the application for a NoSQL database.
others.C: Self-managed MySQL on EC2 increases operational overhead and still uses binlog replication lag.
others.D: Migrating to DynamoDB requires major application changes.

tip: RDS MySQL replica lag problems = Aurora Replicas (shared storage).

why: An Aurora global database replicates storage to the secondary Region with low lag, and the secondary cluster can be headless (no DB instances), so you pay mainly for replicated storage and I/O. Instances are added only during failover, making it the most cost-effective DR replication.

others.A: Binlog replication is more to manage and slower, and keeping an instance running costs more.
others.C: DMS continuous replication requires a replication instance, adding cost and overhead.
others.D: Keeping at least one instance in the secondary Region costs more than a headless secondary.

tip: Cheapest Aurora cross-Region DR = headless global database secondary.

why: Storing the credentials in Secrets Manager removes them from code, and the application retrieves them with a simple SDK call. Secrets Manager provides managed rotation schedules for RDS MySQL using built-in rotation templates, so no custom rotation code is needed.

others.A: KMS stores encryption keys, not database credentials, and key rotation does not rotate DB passwords.
others.B: Writing a custom rotation Lambda is more programming effort than native rotation.
others.D: Parameter Store does not offer automatic credential rotation.

tip: Built-in rotation is the differentiator between Secrets Manager and Parameter Store.

why: AWS WAF attaches to the ALB and its managed rules (such as the SQL database rule group) and SQL injection match statements inspect requests and block SQL injection attempts before they reach the application.

others.B: ALB listener rules cannot detect SQL injection patterns.
others.C: Shield Advanced focuses on DDoS protection; SQL injection blocking is done by WAF rules.
others.D: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities; it does not block requests.
others.F: Empty option text in the source data; not a valid solution.

tip: SQLi/XSS protection = AWS WAF on ALB, API Gateway, CloudFront or AppSync.

why: A Lake Formation blueprint ingests data from the Aurora database into the governed S3 data lake with little effort. Lake Formation then enforces column-level permissions, and QuickSight queries through Athena, which honors those permissions.

others.A: EMR adds cluster management and does not provide governed column-level authorization.
others.B: IAM policies cannot enforce column-level access on data in S3.
others.C: S3 bucket policies cannot control access at the column level, and Glue Elastic Views never became generally available.

tip: Column/row-level permissions on a data lake = Lake Formation, queried via Athena.

why: Predictive scaling uses machine learning on historical CPU utilization to forecast capacity needs automatically, so no one has to analyze trends. Its scheduling buffer can pre-launch instances (here 30 minutes) before the forecast load, meeting the requirement with minimal overhead.

others.A: Dynamic target tracking reacts only after load rises, so capacity is not ready 30 minutes early.
others.B: Scheduled scaling requires someone to choose capacity values, which the company cannot analyze.
others.D: A custom Lambda reacting at 60% CPU is reactive and adds code to maintain.

tip: Recurring pattern but unknown capacity values = predictive scaling.

why: Aurora global database is fully managed and replicates data to a secondary cluster in the DR Region with typically under one second of lag, and supports managed cross-Region failover. This provides multi-Region DR with the least operational overhead.

others.A: Self-managing MySQL replication across EC2 instances is high overhead.
others.B: Multi-AZ and read replicas in other AZs stay within one Region.
others.D: Restoring from replicated backups requires manual work and gives longer RTO and RPO.

tip: Managed multi-Region relational DR = Aurora global database.

why: The Amazon SQS Extended Client Library for Java stores large payloads (up to 2 GB) in S3 and sends a reference pointer through SQS, transparently retrieving them on receive. It is a drop-in client wrapper, so code changes are minimal.

others.B: Option text missing in the source; any alternative messaging service such as EventBridge has similar small payload limits.
others.C: SQS limits cannot be raised to 50 MB (the maximum is now 1 MiB, previously 256 KB).
others.D: SQS cannot natively reference EFS locations, so custom code would be required.

tip: Large SQS payloads = Extended Client Library with S3.

why: Amazon Cognito user pools provide serverless authentication billed per monthly active user (with a free tier that easily covers under 100 users) and scale as the user base grows. Lambda@Edge validates tokens at CloudFront edge locations for low-latency authorization, and CloudFront serves the application globally.

others.B: Managed Microsoft AD is not serverless, is costly for under 100 users, and an ALB is Regional, not global.
others.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads to S3; it does not serve a web application globally, and Regional Lambda adds login latency.
others.D: Managed AD is expensive and not serverless, and Elastic Beanstalk does not serve content globally.

tip: Serverless auth for web/mobile users = Cognito; edge authorization = Lambda@Edge.

why: Amazon S3 File Gateway presents both SMB and NFS file shares to clients while storing files as objects in S3, so S3 Lifecycle policies can tier inactive data. Clients keep the same file share look and feel, with frequently accessed data cached locally.

others.A: Volume Gateway presents iSCSI block volumes, not SMB/NFS shares, and data is not stored as accessible S3 objects for lifecycle rules.
others.B: Tape Gateway emulates tape libraries for backup software.
others.C: FSx File Gateway stores data in FSx for Windows (SMB only), not S3, so S3 Lifecycle policies do not apply.

tip: SMB/NFS shares backed by S3 objects = S3 File Gateway.

why: Compute Savings Plans give up to about 66% savings over 3 years and automatically apply across any instance family, size, Region, OS and tenancy, plus Fargate and Lambda. That flexibility lets the company change instance family and sizes later while still saving.

others.B: EC2 Instance Savings Plans lock you to one instance family in one Region.
others.C: Zonal Reserved Instances are locked to a specific instance type and AZ.
others.D: Standard Reserved Instances cannot change instance family.

tip: Need to change instance family = Compute Savings Plan (or Convertible RIs).

why: For a constant, predictable workload, provisioned capacity mode with specified RCUs and WCUs is cheaper than on-demand and keeps costs fixed and predictable within budget. (Reserved capacity can further discount provisioned throughput.)

others.A: Standard-IA lowers storage cost for rarely accessed tables but raises throughput cost, unsuitable for actively analyzed data.
others.C: On-demand mode does not use RCU/WCU settings and costs more per request for steady traffic.
others.D: Reserved capacity is only available for provisioned mode, not on-demand.

tip: Predictable DynamoDB traffic = provisioned (+ auto scaling / reserved capacity); spiky/unknown = on-demand.

why: A snapshot encrypted with a customer managed KMS key can be shared with another account if the key policy grants that account permission to use the key. Sharing the snapshot and the key keeps the backup encrypted and secure.

others.A: Creating an unencrypted copy of confidential data violates security requirements (and encrypted Aurora snapshots cannot simply be copied to unencrypted).
others.C: Snapshots encrypted with AWS managed keys cannot be shared, and permissions are not granted via aliases.
others.D: RDS/Aurora snapshots cannot be downloaded directly, and this is less secure and more complex.

tip: Share encrypted snapshots: customer managed key + key policy grant + snapshot share.

why: Converting to Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby with automatic failover for high availability. A read replica (supported for RDS SQL Server Enterprise/Standard editions) offloads the occasional reporting queries so transaction posting is not slowed.

others.B: A snapshot restore gives a stale, separate copy with no automatic recovery.
others.D: RDS Custom gives OS-level access but does not by itself provide HA or reporting offload.
others.E: RDS Proxy pools connections; it cannot restrict reports to a maintenance window.

tip: HA = Multi-AZ; read offload = read replica.

why: AWS Step Functions state machines orchestrate distributed workflow steps serverlessly, invoking Lambda functions for each step with built-in retries and error handling. This is event-driven, distributed and has minimal operational overhead.

others.A: AWS Glue is for ETL jobs, not general application workflow orchestration.
others.B: Running steps on EC2 instances is not serverless and adds overhead.
others.C: Scheduled invocations are not an event-driven workflow and lack step orchestration.

tip: Serverless orchestration of multi-step workflows = Step Functions.

why: AWS Global Accelerator supports UDP listeners and routes players onto the AWS global network at the nearest edge location, reducing latency, jitter and packet loss. Endpoint groups in each of the eight Regions provide health-based routing to the closest healthy endpoint.

others.A: Transit gateway peering connects VPCs to each other; it does not optimize end-user paths into AWS.
others.C: This option text is an artifact of the source data, not a solution.
others.D: VPC peering connects VPCs, not users, and there is no setting to turn on UDP.

tip: UDP + global low latency = Global Accelerator (CloudFront is HTTP/HTTPS only).

why: A 1 TB gp2 volume provides a 3,000 IOPS baseline (3 IOPS per GB), covering 1,000 peak IOPS and double that, at far lower cost than io2. RDS Multi-AZ makes the database fully managed, highly available and fault tolerant.

others.A: io2 Block Express provides far more IOPS than needed at much higher cost.
others.C: S3 storage classes are object storage, not a MySQL database tier.
others.D: Self-managed EC2 database instances are not a fully managed solution.

tip: gp2 = 3 IOPS/GiB (burst to 3,000 for small volumes); gp3 = 3,000 IOPS baseline at any size and usually cheaper.

why: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections among many concurrent Lambda invocations, preventing connection exhaustion and timeouts during spikes. It requires only changing the database endpoint, so code changes are minimal.

others.A: Reducing Lambda concurrency throttles the application and causes other failures.
others.C: A larger instance raises connection limits but still cannot absorb unpredictable bursts efficiently and costs more.
others.D: Migrating to DynamoDB requires a major rewrite.

tip: Lambda + RDS connection problems = RDS Proxy.

why: AWS Batch on EC2 can provision instances with 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB of memory, schedule the hourly job, and scale compute down when idle. It is a managed service, so operational overhead is low.

others.A: Lambda is limited to 15 minutes, 10 GB memory and 6 vCPUs, insufficient for this job.
others.B: Fargate tasks max out at 16 vCPU and 120 GB memory, below the required resources.
others.C: Lightsail does not offer instances this large and is not designed for batch scaling.

tip: Large CPU/memory batch jobs = AWS Batch on EC2; Fargate and Lambda have size limits.

why: S3 Standard-IA keeps millisecond access and stores data across at least three AZs with the same 99.99% availability design target class tier (99.9% SLA) and 11 nines durability, at lower storage cost. A lifecycle transition after 30 days (the minimum for Standard-IA) cuts costs for the rarely accessed 75%.

others.A: Glacier Deep Archive requires hours to restore, so data is not immediately accessible.
others.C: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, reducing resiliency.
others.D: One Zone-IA immediately reduces resiliency and incurs costs for frequently accessed new data.

tip: Immediate access + multi-AZ resiliency + infrequent = Standard-IA.

why: Storing static files in S3 and caching them with CloudFront offloads static delivery with high availability. FSx for Windows File Server provides a highly available SMB share that all Windows EC2 instances mount to share the server-side code.

others.B: ElastiCache is an in-memory data cache within a Region, not an edge cache for static files.
others.C: EFS uses NFS and is not supported for Windows instances.
others.E: A gp2 EBS volume cannot be shared across multiple instances.

tip: Windows shared storage = FSx for Windows; Linux = EFS.

why: A Lambda@Edge function associated with the image cache behaviors can resize images and select formats (for example WebP based on the Accept header) at the edge using an image library, and CloudFront caches the results. This is managed and scales automatically with little operational overhead.

others.A: Processing thousands of images per second on self-managed EC2 is high operational overhead.
others.B: Origin request policies control which values are forwarded to the origin; they cannot resize images.
others.D: Response headers policies add or modify headers; they cannot transform images.

tip: On-the-fly image transformation at the edge = Lambda@Edge (or the Dynamic Image Transformation solution).

why: A bucket policy denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false enforces HTTPS for data in transit. SSE-KMS with a customer managed key lets the compliance team administer the key, its policy and rotation for data at rest.

others.A: ACM public certificates cannot be associated with S3, and S3 endpoints already have their own TLS.
others.B: SSE-S3 keys are fully managed by AWS, so the compliance team cannot administer them.
others.D: Macie discovers sensitive data; it does not encrypt data at rest.

tip: Customer-controlled keys = SSE-KMS with a customer managed key; enforce TLS with aws:SecureTransport.

why: Private API Gateway APIs are accessed through an interface VPC endpoint (execute-api, AWS PrivateLink). Using the interface endpoint keeps BuyStock's calls to CheckFunds within the VPC with little or no code change, especially with private DNS enabled.

others.A: An API key header controls authorization and usage plans, not the network path.
others.C: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.
others.D: Adding SQS between the APIs requires significant code redesign.

tip: Gateway endpoints: S3 and DynamoDB only; everything else uses interface endpoints.

why: DynamoDB with DAX delivers microsecond to sub-millisecond read latency for frequently accessed data. DynamoDB's native export to S3 requires no custom code, and Athena runs one-time SQL queries on the exported historical data serverlessly.

others.A: RDS does not provide sub-millisecond reads, and custom export scripts add overhead.
others.B: S3 cannot deliver sub-millisecond reads, and Deep Archive data is not directly queryable.
others.D: DynamoDB alone gives single-digit millisecond (not sub-millisecond) reads, and there is no query solution for historical data.

tip: Sub-millisecond = in-memory cache (DAX for DynamoDB, ElastiCache otherwise).

why: Kinesis Data Streams preserves record order within a shard, and using payment ID as the partition key sends all records for a payment to the same shard. An SQS FIFO queue with the payment ID as message group ID guarantees ordered delivery per payment.

others.A: DynamoDB is a database, not a messaging system that preserves send order.
others.C: Memcached is a cache with no ordering guarantees or durable messaging.
others.D: Empty option text in the source; a standard SQS queue (the original choice) does not guarantee ordering.

tip: Ordering per key: Kinesis partition key or SQS FIFO message group ID.

why: SNS FIFO topics deliver messages in strict order with deduplication and fan out to multiple subscribers concurrently (typically SQS FIFO queues for each service). This meets both the concurrent fan-out to leaderboard, matchmaking and authentication and the ordering guarantee.

others.A: EventBridge does not guarantee event ordering.
others.C: SNS standard topics provide best-effort ordering only.
others.D: An SQS FIFO queue delivers to one consumer group; it does not fan out the same event to several services.

tip: Ordered fan-out = SNS FIFO -> SQS FIFO.

why: Enabling SSE with a customer managed KMS key on both SNS and SQS encrypts data at rest, and a key policy limits which principals can use the key to read the data. Adding an aws:SecureTransport condition in the queue policy enforces TLS in transit.

others.A: SQS-managed or AWS managed keys have default policies that cannot be edited, so key usage cannot be restricted that way.
others.C: The default AWS managed key policy for SNS cannot be modified to restrict principals.
others.E: KMS key access is controlled primarily by the key policy; an IAM policy alone cannot restrict key usage to only the authorized principals.

tip: To control who can use a key, you need a customer managed key and its key policy.

why: RDS automated backups combine daily snapshots with transaction logs uploaded every 5 minutes, enabling point-in-time restore to any second within the retention period (up to 35 days). Setting retention to 30 days allows restoring to 5 minutes before the bad edit.

others.A: Read replicas replicate the accidental change too.
others.B: Manual snapshots capture only specific moments, not any point in time.
others.D: Multi-AZ synchronously replicates the mistake to the standby.

tip: Point-in-time restore (up to 35 days) = automated backups.

why: API Gateway usage plans with API keys let you give subscribed users keys tied to a plan that grants access to the premium API methods, while non-subscribers are rejected. It is built-in configuration with low operational overhead.

others.A: Caching and throttling control performance and rates, not subscription-based access.
others.B: WAF filters by request attributes like IPs or patterns, not user subscription status.
others.C: Fine-grained DynamoDB IAM permissions require per-user credentials (for example via identity pools) and more setup than usage plans.

tip: API keys are for metering/usage plans; for real authorization consider Cognito groups or Lambda authorizers.

why: Global Accelerator supports UDP and routes users over the AWS backbone to the closest healthy endpoint with fast failover. NLBs in each Region can target the on-premises servers by IP address (over VPN/Direct Connect), so the application stays on premises while gaining performance and availability.

others.B: ALBs do not support UDP.
others.C: CloudFront does not support UDP traffic.
others.D: ALBs and CloudFront do not support UDP.

tip: UDP + global performance = Global Accelerator with NLB endpoints.

why: IAM supports a single account-level password policy that sets complexity rules and maximum password age (rotation) for all IAM users. Setting it once applies to all new users and password changes.

others.B: IAM password policies cannot be set per user.
others.C: Third-party software is unnecessary because IAM provides this natively.
others.D: There is no such event-based mechanism to set password requirements; it is far more complex.

tip: IAM password policy is account-wide.

why: AWS Batch runs each task as a containerized job regardless of programming language, provisioning and scaling compute as needed. EventBridge schedules the jobs, removing single-instance bottlenecks with low operational overhead; one-hour tasks fit Batch with no time limit.

others.B: App Runner is for web applications and APIs, not scheduled batch jobs.
others.C: Lambda has a 15-minute maximum, so 1-hour tasks cannot run.
others.D: Cloning the whole instance does not distribute individual tasks and scales inefficiently.

tip: Jobs longer than 15 minutes rule out Lambda.

why: A NAT gateway is a managed, highly available (within an AZ) service that lets private-subnet instances initiate outbound internet connections. It must be placed in a public subnet with a route from private subnets, requiring no patching or maintenance.

others.A: NAT instances are self-managed EC2 instances requiring patching and failover handling.
others.B: A NAT instance in a private subnet cannot reach the internet, and it is self-managed.
others.D: A NAT gateway in a private subnet has no route to an internet gateway.

tip: Managed outbound internet for private subnets = NAT gateway in a public subnet (one per AZ for resilience).

why: Enabling EBS encryption by default with the customer managed key ensures every new EBS volume for the node group is encrypted automatically. Granting the cluster/node role permission to use the KMS key allows volumes to be created and attached with that key.

others.A: A custom Kubernetes plugin adds operational overhead.
others.B: Existing EBS volumes cannot be encrypted in place; they must be recreated from encrypted snapshots.
others.E: KMS keys cannot be exported to store as Kubernetes secrets.

tip: Account/Region-wide EBS encryption by default is the easiest way to enforce encrypted volumes.

why: High-resolution images belong in S3, which scales and is cheap, while DynamoDB stores the geographic code as the key and the S3 URL as the value. DynamoDB scales automatically to tens of thousands of updates and is highly available, making it the most cost-effective option.

others.A: Storing large images in Oracle on RDS is expensive and scales poorly, plus licensing cost.
others.C: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, too small for high-resolution images, and DAX helps reads, not writes.
others.D: Oracle on RDS adds licensing cost and does not scale writes as easily as DynamoDB.

tip: Large binaries in S3, metadata/pointers in a database.

why: Data is used daily for 30 days, so S3 Standard fits initially; afterwards it is accessed only quarterly, so Standard-IA keeps it immediately available at lower cost. After 1 year it moves to Glacier Deep Archive for cheapest archival, all via lifecycle rules.

others.A: With trillions of objects, Intelligent-Tiering's per-object monitoring fees become very costly for a pattern that is already predictable.
others.B: Intelligent-Tiering's archive tiers are not Deep Archive storage class transitions by age, and monitoring fees remain high.
others.C: Standard-IA for brand-new data that is read every day incurs high retrieval charges.

tip: Known access pattern = explicit lifecycle rules; unknown pattern = Intelligent-Tiering.

why: A single Direct Connect connection provides consistent, low-latency bandwidth to the data center and lower data transfer out rates than the internet. A transit gateway attached to all three VPCs (and to Direct Connect via a Direct Connect gateway) handles both inter-VPC and on-premises routing cost-effectively.

others.A: VPNs over the internet do not give consistent latency for hundreds of GB daily and do not connect the VPCs to each other.
others.B: Third-party appliances in each VPC add licensing, instances and management overhead (option text truncated).
others.C: Three Direct Connect connections triple the port cost and still do not provide inter-VPC communication.

tip: Many VPCs + on premises = Transit Gateway + Direct Connect gateway.

why: Step Functions orchestrates Lambda functions and services on EC2, containers or on premises (via activities), and supports human approval steps using callback task tokens. It is serverless with built-in state, retries and error handling.

others.B: Glue jobs are for ETL, not general workflow orchestration with approvals.
others.C: SQS decouples components but provides no workflow orchestration or approval logic.
others.D: Lambda plus EventBridge requires building orchestration and state handling yourself.

tip: Workflow with manual approval = Step Functions callback pattern (waitForTaskToken).

why: RDS Proxy maintains a pool of database connections and multiplexes many short-lived serverless connections onto them, preventing connection rejection during spikes. It is fully managed and only requires pointing applications at the proxy endpoint.

others.B: Memcached caches data but does not manage database connections, and requires code changes.
others.C: Higher I/O capacity does not solve connection exhaustion from bursty serverless clients.
others.D: The Multi-AZ standby cannot accept connections, so it does not add connection capacity.

tip: Serverless apps exhausting DB connections = RDS Proxy.

why: Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks pause instances in Pending:Wait and Terminating:Wait states so a script (for example via EventBridge and Systems Manager or Lambda) can send reports reliably on both launch and termination. This is built in and works for every instance the group launches or terminates.

others.A: A scheduled Lambda misses the exact launch and termination moments and is inefficient.
others.C: User data runs only at launch, not at termination, and launch configurations are deprecated.
others.D: Auto Scaling cannot directly invoke an OS script on termination without lifecycle hooks.

tip: Run actions on scale-out/scale-in events = lifecycle hooks.

why: A Network Load Balancer supports UDP and scales to handle traffic spikes for the game servers. DynamoDB on-demand stores non-relational data like scores and scales automatically without capacity planning or intervention.

others.A: Route 53 is DNS-based and not a load balancer, and Aurora is relational.
others.C: Aurora Global Database is relational and requires capacity management.
others.D: ALBs do not support UDP.

tip: UDP load balancing = NLB; non-relational auto-scaling = DynamoDB on-demand.

why: Loading many libraries causes cold start latency on new Lambda execution environments. Provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of environments initialized and ready, so all users get consistently low latency with just a configuration change.

others.A: Bypassing the API exposes the database and requires major changes.
others.C: Caching query results in S3 adds code and does not address cold starts.
others.D: A bigger database does not reduce Lambda initialization latency.

tip: Lambda cold starts = provisioned concurrency (or SnapStart for Java).

why: A Lambda function that calls the EC2 and RDS start/stop APIs, invoked by EventBridge scheduled rules, is serverless and costs almost nothing to run. It automatically starts and stops resources around business hours with no infrastructure to maintain.

others.A: EC2 has no elastic resize, and RDS instances cannot scale to zero.
others.B: Marketplace solutions may add licensing cost and dependency on a third party.
others.C: An extra EC2 instance running cron adds cost and maintenance.

tip: Scheduled automation without servers = EventBridge Scheduler + Lambda (or Instance Scheduler on AWS).

why: Aurora PostgreSQL is compatible with the existing PostgreSQL application, so code changes are minimal. Directing reporting queries to an Aurora Replica offloads the long relational queries so document writes on the primary are not blocked.

others.A: DocumentDB is a MongoDB-compatible document database, requiring rewriting relational queries.
others.C: The standby in a single-standby Multi-AZ RDS deployment cannot serve read traffic.
others.D: DynamoDB requires a redesign and does not support the existing relational queries.

tip: A classic Multi-AZ standby is not readable; use read replicas or Multi-AZ DB clusters.

why: A TLS listener on the NLB with a server certificate (for example from ACM) encrypts client traffic in transit and terminates TLS at the load balancer. This directly improves data-in-transit security for the sensor traffic.

others.B: Empty option text in the source data; not a valid solution.
others.C: Switching to an ALB with WAF protects against web exploits but does not by itself encrypt data in transit.
others.D: EBS encryption protects data at rest, not in transit.

tip: In transit = TLS listeners/certificates; at rest = KMS encryption.

why: Socket- and core-based BYOL licensing requires Dedicated Hosts, which expose physical sockets and cores. With predictable capacity and uptime, reserving the Dedicated Hosts gives the largest discount, making Dedicated Reserved Hosts most cost-effective.

others.B: On-Demand Dedicated Hosts support BYOL but cost more than reserved for steady usage.
others.C: Dedicated Instances do not provide visibility into sockets and cores for licensing.
others.D: Dedicated On-Demand Instances lack socket/core visibility and cost more.

tip: Per-socket/per-core BYOL = Dedicated Hosts.

why: EFS Standard is a POSIX-compliant shared file system that stores data across multiple AZs for high availability and maximum durability. A lifecycle management policy moves files not accessed for 30 days to EFS Standard-IA, reducing cost.

others.A: S3 is object storage and not POSIX-compliant, and Glacier is not readily accessible.
others.B: S3 is not a POSIX-compliant shared file system.
others.D: EFS One Zone stores data in a single AZ, reducing availability and durability.

tip: POSIX shared storage across AZs = EFS Standard with lifecycle to IA.
